actions: stabilizes humeral head in glenoid (rotator cuff)

functional_compartments.name: Single homogeneous fiber population (no documented sub-compartmentalization)
functional_compartments.function_note: Smallest, most laterally-placed rotator cuff muscle; unlike its cuff neighbors, no independently-innervated sub-compartments have been documented.
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell)

trigger_points.location_description: Point in the belly along the axillary (lateral) border of the scapula, just caudal-lateral to the infraspinatus trigger points
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Sharply localised deep pain at the posterior deltoid region near its insertion (a ‘silver-dollar’-sized area); may be accompanied by paraesthesia of the 4th-5th fingers (ulnar-mimic) without objective deficit.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Pain reaching backwards/up behind the back; end-range internal-rotation stretch; usually little frank weakness unless axillary neuropathy is also present.
trigger_points.notes: Typically found together with infraspinatus trigger points rather than alone. The finger-paraesthesia association is a clinical observation only, without controlled data -- flagged as such in this atlas's source document's verification appendix.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons Trigger Point Manual -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded shoulder muscle reference document (Donnelly JM, Fernandez-de-las-Penas C, Finnegan M, Freeman JL (eds), Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual, 3rd ed., Wolters Kluwer, 2019)

clinical.function_biomechanics: External rotation, most effective with the arm abducted/elevated (posterior cuff force couple with subscapularis); compresses and depresses the head; resists antero-superior translation; ~10% of cuff moment. Often hypertrophies and becomes the last functioning external rotator in massive posterosuperior cuff tears (its integrity predicts function after reverse arthroplasty and tendon transfers).
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: No named constant bursa; the subdeltoid extension of the subacromial bursa lies superficial to its tendon. Adjacent structures — mutual influence: Forms the superior border of the quadrangular space (axillary n. + posterior circumflex humeral a.) and of the triangular space (circumflex scapular a.): fibrous bands/hypertrophy here cause quadrilateral space syndrome — posterior shoulder pain and point tenderness, worse in abduction–external rotation, with possible teres minor±deltoid denervation. Deltoid covers it; posterior capsule adherent.

trigger_points.location: TrP in the belly along the axillary border, just caudal-lateral to infraspinatus points; typically found with infraspinatus TrPs rather than alone.
trigger_points.referred_pain: Sharply localised deep pain at the posterior deltoid region near its insertion (“silver-dollar” area); may be accompanied by paraesthesia of the 4th–5th fingers (ulnar-mimic) without objective deficit — evidence is clinical-observational.
trigger_points.source: Donnelly JM, Fernández-de-las-Peñas C, Finnegan M, Freeman JL (eds). Travell, Simons & Simons’ Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual. 3rd ed. Wolters Kluwer; 2019. Muscle chapters as named in each section.

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: Into its territory (posterior deltoid area): subscapularis (main mimic), teres major, latissimus, supraspinatus rarely, triceps long head, posterior deltoid TrPs, levator scapulae
quadrilateral-space syndrome and posterior labral/capsular pathology
clinical.movement_restrictions_aggravators: Pain reaching backwards/up behind the back; end-range internal rotation stretch pain; usually little frank weakness unless axillary neuropathy.
clinical.notes: Posterior point tenderness + AER provocation → think quadrilateral space (Cahill); atrophy visible on sagittal MRI as a fatty teres minor with intact infraspinatus suggests axillary-branch lesion.
clinical.caveat: Trigger-point locations and referral maps derive from the Travell–Simons clinical-observational tradition, now standardised by Delphi consensus criteria [32] and supported by prevalence and hyperalgesia studies in shoulder pain [30,31]; they are expert-level evidence, not trial-level, and inter-examiner reliability of TrP palpation is moderate. Facet, ACJ and subacromial referral patterns, by contrast, come from experimental provocation in volunteers/patients [33,34,37]. Textbook anatomy is cited at section level; where major texts disagree (segmental levels), the range is given and flagged. Figures and patterns older than 12 months are anatomical/physiological constants and are not considered stale.
